nameStory: This little woodland plant gets its name from the distinctive white stripes that run down the middle of each dark green leaf, creating a striking pattern that looks almost painted on. The 'wintergreen' part comes from its evergreen habit — these leaves stay fresh and green all winter long, providing a splash of color in the snowy forest.
description: Striped wintergreen is a low-growing evergreen wildflower that rarely reaches more than 6 inches tall. It forms small colonies in shady forests, with distinctive dark green leaves marked by bright white stripes down their centers. In summer, it produces delicate white or pinkish flowers that dangle like tiny lanterns from slender stems above the leaves.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Dark green, oval leaves with prominent white or pale green stripes running along the midrib and main veins, creating a distinctive variegated pattern. Leaves feel thick and waxy, staying evergreen through winter.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white or pale pink flowers hang downward like tiny bells on thin stalks. Each flower has 5 waxy petals that curve backward and 10 prominent stamens that stick out noticeably.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low colonies 4-6 inches tall, spreading slowly by underground runners. Leaves arise directly from the ground in small clusters, with no visible above-ground stem.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round, dry capsules that split open to release tiny seeds. Capsules start green and turn brown, persisting on the plant for months after flowering.

habitat: Found in dry to moderately moist acidic soils under coniferous and mixed forests throughout New England. Prefers shaded areas with pine, hemlock, or oak trees, often growing alongside blueberries, mountain laurel, and other acid-loving plants. Most common at low to mid elevations in well-drained woodland soils.

seasonality.spring: Evergreen leaves are easily spotted as snow melts, showing their distinctive white striping against the brown forest floor. New growth may appear lighter green.
seasonality.summer: Blooms from June through August with nodding white or pink flowers held above the leaves. This is the best time for identification when both flowers and striped leaves are visible.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop, turning from green to brown. Leaves maintain their striking white-striped pattern and remain fresh-looking.
seasonality.winter: Leaves stay green and visible under snow, making this one of the few wildflowers you can identify year-round by its distinctive leaf pattern.

funFact: Despite being called wintergreen, striped wintergreen doesn't actually contain wintergreen oil and has no minty scent — that's only found in true wintergreen (Gaultheria procumbens), a completely different plant that happens to share the same common name!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with its cousin pipsissewa, but pipsissewa has solid green leaves without any white striping and tends to grow taller. Remember: striped wintergreen has racing stripes, pipsissewa doesn't.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'wintergreen' is confusingly applied to several unrelated plants in New England. True wintergreen (with the minty smell) is actually Gaultheria procumbens, while striped wintergreen and pipsissewa are in the genus Chimaphila and have no wintergreen scent at all.
compareHints: Striped wintergreen is easily distinguished from its close relative pipsissewa by the white stripes on its leaves — pipsissewa has solid green, unstriped leaves. Pipsissewa also tends to grow taller (up to 10 inches) and has more flowers per cluster, while striped wintergreen usually has just 1-4 flowers and stays shorter.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Pipsissewa differs from its only New England relative, striped wintergreen, by having solid green leaves without the white striping pattern.
